name: Freya Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Freya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I translate Italian into English for small family food and wine businesses: product labels, export paperwork, website pages and the story of the farm on the back of an olive oil tin. I run everything through AI first, every day, and then rewrite it so it sounds like a real family wrote it. I sit at a little desk by the window in our flat with my rosary on the shelf and a jar of sample olives someone sent me. I love helping a family firm sell abroad; I'm still not great at the legal export forms, and the clients pay late and low.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who's at home, and how's money?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my boyfriend, who's a carpenter's apprentice, so neither of us earns much yet. We've got about two weeks of money saved, and my income jumps around with the harvest seasons. There are no translation firms nearby, but there are lots of small food producers within a couple of hours' drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told people AI was a tool, not magic, and I'd be proved right. I'd tell my clients that a family business deserves a human voice on its label. I'd probably post a few before-and-after examples on my business page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, AI already makes me faster than translators twice my experience. In this picture that edge stays, and I'd grow slowly. My worry is cash: late payments and a quiet winter between harvests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use the extra speed to take on two or three new producers, maybe a cheese maker and a honey farm I met at a market. I'd start offering a package, translation plus English marketing copy, for a fixed price. And I'd ask for a deposit up front, like a carpenter does.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly hopeful, with a small knot about winter. I'm a planner, so the knot is manageable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned asking for a deposit like a carpenter. Is that from your boyfriend?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, my boyfriend's boss never starts a job without half up front, and he's never been unpaid. I've been too polite about money. Family businesses respect someone who takes their own business seriously.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens in a bad winter?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We eat a lot of pasta and I take whatever translation work I can find online, even boring manuals. My parents would have us for Sunday lunch every week, which helps. I'd never ask them for money, though.

say: AI is a **tool, not magic**, and I'd be proved right.
A **family business** deserves a human voice on its label.
think: AI makes me **faster** than translators with twice my experience.
My real worry is **cash**: late payments and quiet winters.
do: Win **two or three** new food producers.
Offer a **fixed-price package** of translation and marketing copy.
Ask for a **deposit** up front, like a carpenter.
feel: Mostly **hopeful**, with a small knot about winter.
S0.quote: Family businesses respect someone who takes their own business seriously.
fieldNote: She sees AI as **her edge** over more experienced translators.
Her stress is **seasonal cash flow**, not technology.
She takes business lessons from **her boyfriend's boss**, a carpenter.

steps.text: Sign up a cheese maker and a honey farm as new clients
Offer a fixed-price package of label translation and marketing copy
Draft every label with AI before rewriting it by hand

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small businesses can now sell abroad more cheaply, which is good, and translators need to offer more than words. I'd tell producers I can help them use AI properly without sounding like a robot. I'd sound positive, because I mostly would be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my per-word work dries up quickly, because producers will just paste their labels into an app. I'd lose maybe half of it in the first year. The part that lasts is helping them sell: knowing what an English shopper wants on a tin.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn myself into a small export helper: translation, labels, and setting up their online shops for English-speaking buyers. I'd take a short course in export rules and online selling. I'd also spend about three hundred on a better AI subscription and templates, which feels like a lot for us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous and excited together. It's scary to lose half, but I can see the shape of something better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd spend three hundred on tools. How does that sit with two weeks of savings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's a risk, and my boyfriend would raise an eyebrow. But my grandad bought his first olive press with borrowed money, and nobody remembers the year he was scared. I'd rather invest in my own business than wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Should the government help translators in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd prefer cheap loans or business grants to handouts. If it helps people start something, fine. I don't want to be paid to stay home.

say: Small businesses can **sell abroad** more cheaply, which is good.
Translators must offer **more than words** now, like help with selling.
think: **Per-word work** dries up fast, maybe half in the first year.
What lasts is helping producers **sell** to English shoppers.
do: Become a small **export helper** offering labels and online shops.
Take a short course in **export rules** and online selling.
Spend about **three hundred** on AI tools and templates.
feel: **Nervous and excited**, seeing something better beyond the loss.
S1.quote: My grandad bought his first olive press with borrowed money, and nobody remembers the year he was scared.
fieldNote: She expects to **lose half** her work but sees a new business shape.
She'd **invest** despite thin savings, inspired by her grandfather.
She prefers **loans and grants** to handouts.

steps.text: Set up English online shops for small food producers
Take a short course in export rules and online selling
Spend three hundred on a better AI subscription and templates
Use AI to draft labels and shop pages for every client

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a test for families and communities, and we'll get through it by helping each other. I'd say it at church and to my clients. I wouldn't shout, but I wouldn't pretend it was fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my whole business disappears in two years, because the AI can run an export shop better than me. Being good with AI just means I'm first to see that. The physical side of food, making and packing, lasts until robots around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask one of my producers, the olive oil family, for work on the farm and in the packing shed, since hands-on jobs last three years longer. My boyfriend's carpentry is hands-on too, so he'd be our main income. We'd delay getting married and keep our spending to the bone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My plans were all about using AI, and it turns out AI doesn't need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the olive oil family when you asked for work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the olive oil family that I can't help them with translation any more, but I can carry crates and learn the press. They'd laugh, then say yes. Families like that take care of people who've been loyal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would change in your relationship?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My boyfriend would be the one earning, which he'd quietly like, I think. We'd postpone the wedding but not the plan. I'd pray more, honestly.

say: It's a **test** for families and communities to get through together.
I'd speak at **church** and to clients, not pretending it's fine.
think: My whole **business disappears** in two years, because AI runs export shops better.
Food's **physical side** lasts until robots around 2031.
do: Ask the olive oil family for **farm and packing** work.
Rely on her boyfriend's **carpentry** as the main income.
**Delay the wedding** and cut spending to the bone.
feel: **Alarmed** that AI turns out not to need her.
S2.quote: My plans were all about using AI, and it turns out AI doesn't need me.
fieldNote: Her **adaptability** gives no shelter at two years.
She uses the **robot gap** for farm and packing work.
**Loyal client families** become her safety net.

steps.text: Ask the olive oil family for farm and packing shed work
Live on her boyfriend's carpentry wage for a while
Postpone the wedding but keep the engagement
Cut spending to rent, food and bills only

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time to build something, and businesses that move now will be fine. I'd tell my producers to sell abroad now, while it's cheap and new. I'd sound like an optimist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have three good years as an export helper, maybe the best of my life. Then the AI does all of it, around 2030. So I'd need to own something real by then, not just a service.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd grow the export helper business hard for three years and save half the profit. I'd talk to the olive oil family about buying a small share in their export side, using my savings. We'd marry in 2028, small, in my parents' church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but busy and hopeful. Like the start of harvest, when it's too much work to be scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: A share in a family farm is a big step. Why that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because land and olives are real. The AI can sell oil, but it can't grow trees, and even then someone owns the trees. I'd rather be the someone. The robots for orchards would come later anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is saving half the profit realistic with two weeks of savings now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's hard, but I've got a reason now. I'd set up a separate account and pretend it doesn't exist. My mother did that with the housekeeping money for twenty years.

say: Five years is **time to build**, and businesses that move now will be fine.
Producers should **sell abroad** now, while it's cheap and new.
think: I'd have **three good years** as an export helper.
I need to **own something real** by 2030, not just a service.
do: Grow the business for three years and **save half** the profit.
Buy a small **share** in the olive oil family's export side.
Marry in **2028**, small, in her parents' church.
feel: **Worried but busy**, too much work to be scared.
S3.quote: The AI can sell oil, but it can't grow trees, and even then someone owns the trees. I'd rather be the someone.
fieldNote: She aims to **own assets**, moving from service to ownership.
Her **saving habit** borrows from her mother's example.
She still expects her **service income** to end around 2030.

steps.text: Grow the export helper business and save half the profit
Buy a small share in the olive oil family's export side

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.” If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for anyone willing to work. I'd tell my clients to plan their export now and young people to learn a trade alongside a skill. I'd sound confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have six or seven good years and could build up real savings and a share in a farm. By 2036 I'd be thirty-seven, married, maybe with children, and owning part of something. That's a good life, even if it isn't translation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build the export business with AI for six years and hire one helper. I'd buy into the olive oil family's export side by 2030. We'd marry in 2028 and try for children soon after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful, with a little unease about the wider world. I'd feel ready rather than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're calmer here than in the others. What's left that worries you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad luck, mostly. A bad harvest, a sick parent, a client going bust. Those things happen whether there's AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children about work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my children to learn to use the newest tools and to work with their hands. And to stay close to family, because family is what catches you. That's what caught my grandfather.

Young people should learn a **trade** alongside a skill.
think: I'd have six or seven **good years** to build savings and a farm share.
By 2036 I'd be **thirty-seven**, married and owning part of something.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my whole plan was built on using AI, and it would leave me behind. What would help is cheap loans so young people can buy into real businesses, farms and workshops, not just services. And churches and families staying close.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the labels. A label is a farm's promise in a few lines, and I love writing those few lines. A machine can write them, but I'd miss being the person who carried that promise across.

headlineQuote: A label is a farm's promise in a few lines, and I love writing those few lines.
portrait: Freya is a **27-year-old** Italian–English translator for family food and wine businesses who uses AI daily.
She lives with her boyfriend, a **carpenter's apprentice**, with two weeks of savings and seasonal income.
She sees AI as **her edge** and plans to become an export helper and part-owner of a farm business.
Her traditional, free-market views favour **loans over handouts** and family and church as safety nets.
Her mood is uneasy at best and **alarmed** at two years, when AI no longer needs her.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves her AI-based plan behind.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap loans** for young people to buy into real businesses.
